utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, Thomas Laugel, and Simona Onicel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell, and our intern, Ivan Kochovski. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury, should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you stand for a moment and read the solemn declaration. The Court Usher will give you the text of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you tell us your name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vilim Karlovic, born on the 27th of October --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 27 October 1970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karlovic. Mr. Stringer, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karlovic. Can you hear me and understand me?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, can I hear you and I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, do you recall being here at the Tribunal and giving evidence in the Mrksic case, the case involving Messrs. Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic on the 20th and 21st of March, 2006?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And have you recently had an opportunity to listen to the audio recording of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Approximately a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And for the record, the English transcripts of that evidence are at 65 ter 04502 and 04503. They're both confidential. And also for the record, Mr. President, public redacted versions of those transcripts have been uploaded as well. Now, Mr. Karlovic, when -- after you listened to that audio testimony from the Mrksic case, did we have an opportunity to meet then, and did you indicate that there were some corrections or modifications that you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We met a day later, and on that occasion, we made certain amendments and corrections to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And at this time I'd like to ask you to -- I'd like to take you through those so that we can get the record correct on -- on those items. The first of which, Mr. Karlovic, if I understood correctly you wanted to modify your evidence about where it was in Vukovar where you removed your uniform when you were going to enter into the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges, please, what is the correction or the change you'd like to make on that point.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'd only like to say that I removed my military uniform at the hospital itself once I got to the hospital, and I put it away in a room where there were other old, torn uniforms belonging to other people. That's where I put my uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, for the record, Mr. President. The references in the Mrksic testimony now that are being modified are at page 6321, line 23, and 6322, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, in the Mrksic case, had you indicated that you took your uniform off previously at a different location?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I remember correctly, I mentioned a devastated house. I think it was supposed to be the police station that had been burned down in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next modification or clarification, Mr. Karlovic, related to the time that you and your unit were based at this silo in Vukovar. And this is page 6316, line 25, and page 6317, line 1 of the Mrksic testimony. Mr. Karlovic, if I understand correctly, you just wanted to indicate that although you were based at the silo, your unit made interventions in other parts of the town of Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I only want to add that we were stationed at the silo at the time, but with one group we went on several occasions on larger intervention missions in different parts of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we'll actually look at the location of the silo a bit later in your evidence today. Another modification, Mr. Karlovic, and this is at page 6228, line 12 of the Mrksic evidence, there, Mr. Karlovic, you had indicated that you didn't see any other soldiers in the cellar of the Vukovar Hospital and that you wanted to make a clarification on that point.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw some. In fact, some had come with me and there were other soldiers in the basement of that hospital with us. I just wanted to add that I had seen some other people. They were close to me. And I need to add those soldiers did not have any weapons. They were in the same situation as me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then from Mrksic page 6328, you had said that you had been asked whether anything significant happened on the 19th of November, and you indicated no. And there was actually now one point you wanted to add about the 19th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's important to note that a man who was working at the hospital who worked as a technician in the plaster room who applied plaster-casts was removed from the hospital on the 19th - his name was Marko - and he was never seen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall who removed him?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I know people mentioned that the enemy army took him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at page 6330, line 21 of your Mrksic evidence, Mr. Karlovic, you had said that there were only men on your bus; that is, the bus that you were on when you went from the hospital to the barracks and then out to Ovcara. Did you want to correct that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would add there was a married couple, which means there was one woman on the bus. They sat in front of me, just behind the driver. They were already on the bus when we started boarding the bus from the yard of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I do. They were Serbs. Because several times they insisted they were Serbs and should be released. That's why it remained in my memory that they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you know what became of them?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were released at Ovcara, just before the rest of us got off the bus. An officer had come to collect them, and he let them go on their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at page 6332 and 6333 of the Mrksic evidence, you made a reference to someone who you named as Ivan Gruber. Do you want to correct that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's just the correction to the name. It's not Ivan; it's Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Home Guards Corps, the 1st Brigade to which I also belonged but a different unit inside that brigade. He was wounded in his right shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then at line 6337 [sic] from the Mrksic case, you said that you learned that you were at this place called Ovcara farm, that you learned that the name was -- was Ovcara when you were actually at that location. Did you want to modify that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to add that I first heard about Ovcara on the bus itself, from the man who was sitting next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And, again, just so the Chamber understands - and we'll talk about it more later - did you know the area of -- of the Vukovar region at the time that these events occurred?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know the area of Vukovar, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Vukovar for the first time during the war. Otherwise, I'd always lived in Zagreb. I'd never been to Vukovar before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now at page 6339, lines 6 through 9 of your Mrksic evidence, you said that you thought there were about ten people forming this gauntlet that you and the others went through on their way into the hangar at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I gave my estimate, around ten people. It could have been 15. That's the number that I remember roughly. But as we had to go through that gauntlet before entering the hangar, there could have been perhaps 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The last one is at page 6336, lines 1 through 5, Mr. Karlovic, in the Mrksic case, you spoke about a sixth bus that you associated with the JNA barracks. We'll talk about this more in your evidence as well. But the question was whether the sixth bus that you recall also went from the barracks to Ovcara with the other buses.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to say now is that I'm sure he stayed behind us at the barracks. I'm not sure he left for Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Karlovic, having made these corrections or modifications to your evidence in the Mrksic case, are you now able to affirm if the testimony you gave in that case is -- is truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I asked you all the same questions today that you were asked in that case, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that in 90 per cent -- 95 per cent of cases I would give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Prosecution tenders the witness's Rule 92 ter statement, which is 65 ter 4502 and 4503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3000 and P3001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just for the record, and we'll get to this later as well, one other revision, the witness wanted to just make a slight revision of the markings he made on one of the aerial photographs, and our proposal is not to tender that one photograph from the Mrksic case as part of the associated exhibits, and that's 65 ter 2683. But, rather, just to start again with a fresh one and have the witness make the marking that he now would like to make, just so that we're not having to correct a previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, before we talk about the events from late 1991, just a couple of background questions. Did you join the Croatian National Guard in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Not quite 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And later on, then, did the Croatian National Guard sort of become the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Until 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then were you pensioned in 2003 from the -- the army?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was pensioned off in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karlovic, could you give the Judges just a brief description of why you were pensioned at that period. You were still relatively young.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: One of the main reason for the pension was the post-traumatic stress disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, are you currently serving a prison sentence at a place called Lepoglava in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, again, could I ask you just to give us a brief description of why you're currently imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm imprisoned for murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is there any more information you'd like to give us about that or ... I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief. I killed my best man. I mean, I was his best man at his wedding. I borrowed money from him, and I returned it several times over. However, the threats did not stop to me and my family. The threats mentioned that my family and I would be killed. And after a lot of time full of pressure and threats, and after I went bankrupt, in the midst of a quarrel, I fired a gun at the man and took his life. That's why I was imprisoned for six years. That the briefest I can put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That happened on the 30th of October, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karlovic, in your Mrksic evidence, you talk about your arrival at Vukovar. And just a couple questions on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could have, please, on the screen tab 12, which is 65 ter 2680.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. If each one takes that much long to load, Mr. President, we're going to be here for a little while. The next one is 2676. I don't known if there's a way to queue it up while we talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, this is an exhibit that you marked on when you were here in the Mrksic case. And just so the Judges can see, can you describe what this is, what does this show.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This is the direction in which our unit moved from a placed called Bogdanovci, which is marked as A, until we entered the city; and the silo, which is marked as B. We called it the corn field road. That's how we entered Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what was the date of your arrival, then, at this location B?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That was already the 1st October, between 3.00 and 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now the next one is tab 9, which is 65 ter 2676. Okay, Witness. This again is a map showing markings that you made. And you had clarified already in your Mrksic testimony about making interventions from the area of the silo. Again, could you just briefly tell the Judges what this map shows.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We see the position of the silo marked as A. And after that, we see the position to which my unit was moved; that's position B.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's, then, a position squarely within the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's position B.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is this the location you and your colleagues were at, then, when you surrendered or when the resistance ended and you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. That was an initial position. We were losing those positions. And when our resistance stopped, we were closer to the hospital. We were in the vicinity of the hospital. I don't know. If this is not clear enough, we can go through it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STINGER
utterances.text: Just for the Registrar, I can say that the next slide will be 65 ter 2877, which is tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Karlovic, let me ask you some questions then. You just mentioned going to the hospital. Do you recall when it was you arrived at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: On -- on the 17th November, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you why you didn't try to escape Vukovar rather than laying down your weapon and surrendering, perhaps trying to get back out through the corn field through which you had entered.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll have to explain this at greater length. First of all, I should say that probably until the very end of my life I will not have an answer to that question. We were fighting. We had put up a resistance practically until the very last day. Our last positions were around the hospital, and everybody was confused. Some people wanted to stay, other people wanted to leave. Since, in the hospital, I had eight of my wounded fellow combatants, I thought that it was best for me to go to the hospital and to surrender, together with them. I somehow felt safer close to them. However, I also have to state a fact. Perhaps I was fed up with fighting in general, and the uncertainty involved. Perhaps I took the path of least resistance. And, quite simply, I succumbed to my state and stayed at the hospital. This is a complex emotional question. In these moments I did not know the terrain. I was not from Vukovar. I didn't know where I would go. Quite simply at that moment that was the decision I made and probably, as I said, I'll be thinking about it to the end of my life, wondering whether I should have done something different. Now that I survived all of that and that I am alive, I believe that somebody else decided for me to make that decision and I believe that that is God Almighty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karlovic, you mentioned that you had others, other fighters that -- that were in your unit who were wounded and in the hospital. Did any of your comrades in arms end up on the bus with you when you left the hospital and headed off towards the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Zeljko Major was with me and Zoran Gruber as well. Actually, Gruber was not from the basic group that I arrived with but he was a member of that unit, the 1st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately what time it was when you left the hospital and the procedure then began for boarding the buses. In this -- well, can you tell us what date that was.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we started leaving the hospital on the 20th of October. I remember that the whole procedure started around 9.00 in the morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karlovic, we have the transcript, I don't know whether you or -- what was the date?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I probably said the 20th of October, right? First of all, that is the date on which I got married to my wife. Sorry. And that's why it's probably in my mind. I do apologise. I meant to say the 20th of November. The 20th of November at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time it was, then, when the buses arrived at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can remember that it was roughly around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And how many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Five buses that were full.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could now have, please, tab 23, page 14, which is from 65 ter 2877. Page 14. Do you recognise this place, Mr. Karlovic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The barracks in Vukovar where we were with those five buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in just a couple of minutes, I'm going to ask you to take the pen and to make some markings on this. But before I do that, I'd like to ask you just to briefly describe the scene that -- that was taking place during the time that you were there. What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we arrived in the barracks, and as we travelled through town, the enemy army escorted us with different units. The escort, and also the way we were met at the Vukovar barracks, all of it was very hostile, accompanied by threats. They said that they would kill us, slaughter us. So we were very frightened as we were on these buses in the barracks for a couple of hours. Of course these were mixed units of the JNA, the Territorial Defence, Chetnik formations. They were all going around the buses. Some of them wanted to enter the buses immediately. Later on, they did. So it was a situation of general fear, uncertainty. That is what I can say roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you observe any people being taken off the buses?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. After a while, they started taking people out of these five buses. Quite simply, the procedure was as follows: One officer went around the buses, and he carried a list, and on the basis of that list, he took people out of our buses and moved them to this sixth bus that was in the barracks when we arrived. The point was that, in addition to this JNA officer who was getting people out, on the basis of that list, these local Chetniks also took people out of these five buses of ours. They took a few people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you observe what happened to people who were taken off by Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to say what happened to these people. All the people who got out were tortured by the JNA and by the Chetniks. The only difference was that people who were taken out by the JNA were taken to that bus. Of course they were beaten in front of the bus and on the bus itself, whereas those who were taken out of -- taken out by the Chetniks, were immediately beaten as they got off the bus. They were taken behind that hangar. Again, moans could be heard, and swearing, gun-shot, screams. That is what I can say briefly, how people who were taken off our buses were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did these buses remain there at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately we left the barracks around 2.30, 20 minutes to 3.00, something like that. Over three hours for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karlovic, with the assistance of the usher, I'm going to ask if you could take the pen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. Before carrying on, I would like to ask a clarification. Could you please ask the witness about page number 14 of the transcript, because he was talking about members of the JNA who were taken -- who were taking people from the buses. But he also mentioned Chetniks. So what does the witness mean exactly when he uses the word "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, perhaps I could ask you in responding to Judge Mindua's question, could -- to describe in general the criteria that you use when distinguishing between JNA, Chetniks, and TO, which you've all mentioned now.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before I answer, I have to express an opinion of mine, if possible. Throughout my testimony, these four or five times when I was here, I always have to explain who is who and I understand that. Quite simply, we from that part of the world know exactly who was who, but I'll explain it in the briefest possible terms. The easiest way to distinguish between the two was by the way they were dressed and their general appearance, their uniforms, and so on. So this was the main distinction between the JNA, the Chetnik formations. Of course the Territorial Defence was there too. And it was somewhere between the JNA and the Chetnik formations. Of course, it is not always possible. It was not always possible to recognise exactly who belonged to -- to a Territorial Defence unit or a Chetnik unit. JNA members bore the insignia of the former Yugoslavia, five-pointed star. The Territorial Defence had Serbian insignia. And the Chetnik units had their traditional Chetnik emblem, the kokarde, so we could tell them apart. Also they wore their traditional caps, the fur caps, and the Sajkaca caps, and so on, so we could distinguish on that basis who belonged to who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karlovic, with the assistance of the usher, could you first make a marking on the map to show us the position of the five buses, as you recall it. Just the five.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Could you just put a letter A close by that.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you now indicate the location of this -- the green bus, the -- the other bus that the prisoners from the list were put onto.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you give that a letter B.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a place -- you mentioned a hangar where the Chetniks were taking people. Could you indicate the location that you were describing there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Letter C or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Letter C, yes.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now that's the hangar. Were they taken inside the hangar or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Can I draw an arrow to depict the direction in which they took them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very good. And then, finally, Mr. Karlovic, if you could -- if you're able to indicate, again with an arrow, the location from which you entered the barracks, when you came from the hospital, and then also the direction when you left the barracks on your way to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This is the direction we took going to the barracks. The pen is not exactly working the way I'd like it to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you put a letter D next to that.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that's the entry. And then for the exit.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] The same exit, but we just went in this direction, as we went to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the exit, then, that would be letter E.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then just to make sure the record's clear, Mr. Karlovic, the letter C with the hangar, were the witnesses taken to the side or -- of this hangar, as far as you saw -- sorry, not the witnesses. The prisoners.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not quite understand. Yes, C marks the hangar. And the prisoners were taken behind that hangar. Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That is the question and you've given the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender this photograph with its markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, as indicated in your evidence, then, the group moved from this location, the barracks, out to the place that -- yeah, you can put the pen down. Moved out to a place that you learned was called Ovcara. As the buses arrived at Ovcara, which bus were you in? The first, or the last, or something in between?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a column of five buses that was escorted by the military, in front of us, behind us. I was located on the fourth bus, the one-but-last. That is what I have to say about arrival in Ovcara. This transportation did not take very long. We got there relatively quickly. The buses were in a column. And one by one, they approached the Ovcara hangar. People disembarked from these buses, one by one. They passed through this line, or, rather, they ran this gauntlet of about 15 enemy soldiers. Should I say something more about that or should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions. Because the Judges do have now the transcript of your Mrksic evidence, I'd like to focus, Mr. Karlovic, on some of the things, statements that were said or that you overheard while you were there. In your evidence, you've described your -- striking up a conversation with a person you called Stuka. And in -- let me ask you, and in your evidence, you indicate that it's this person Stuka who then came with his captain and took you out of the hangar after you had run through the gauntlet. My question is: In your discussions with Stuka during the time you were at Ovcara, did he make any statements to you about what would be the fate of the people in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I talked to Stuka, and I asked him what would happen to us. And he said, quite simply, that everybody would be killed, that they would kill all of us. And that is what I could say in the briefest possible terms. This man was a JNA soldier. He took me out of this hangar after I had run the gauntlet, after I was beaten, was hit a few times again, and then I was taken out and rescued. As for this relationship with Stuka, I found out from the him that all of us would be killed, and that was the plan for the entire group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now during the time that you were in the hangar did you become aware of another prisoner who was there whose name was Sinisa Glavasevic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon I entered the hangar, on the right-hand side there was Sinisa Glavasevic. That is the moment when they were doing all sorts of things to him, beating him. I know they were screaming with delight, That is Sinisa Glavasevic. He is the greatest Ustasha of all. He killed most of us. I can add that he was radio journalist who reported every day about enemy losses. So that was probably some kind of irony with which they treated him. So I remember this very well as they took all of that out on Sinisa Glavasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During the time that beatings were taking place in the hangar were there any changes of personnel or did the same people continue on the beatings?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, it has to do with the way in which they did this. It was the same group that was there all the time but they were divided into some kind of groups. Since the beatings went on for quite a while, there were two groups. When given a sign, it was a whistle, it was one group that would beat people and then after that the other group would start beating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you observe who had the whistle or who was giving this sign?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see that. I just heard that, as I stood in front of that wall, in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after you were taken out of the hangar by Stuka, then, were you there with other people who also had been put there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to myself, there were six other people; that is to say, there were seven of us in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now during this time, Mr. Karlovic, did you observe that any children or young people were also taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember one particular situation. A mother had arrived in that hangar. I will never know how it was that she found out that something was happening there. I've slowed down a bit because all of this is being interpreted. She was crying and she said that her son was there, that he was born with a disability, that he had nothing to do with the war whatsoever. And I know that a JNA officer took that child out. He had already been beaten up very badly. Before the mother left with that child, she started thanking that officer. And I remember that he said to her, Remember that your son's life was saved by -- and now I keep struggling with this last name. Now is it Ivanovic, Jovanovic, Ivankovic. At any rate, that's what he said, Remember that such and such a person saved your child's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How long did you and these six others in your group there in front of the hangar remain out front observing these events?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my estimate is that it must have been two hours because before we left this hangar, it started getting dark. That is to say, it was winter-time, so realistically speaking it could have been about 5.30 already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then when you left Ovcara, where did you go and how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a white van arrived at Ovcara, and the seven of us squeezed into it. First, we were taken to the Velepromet warehouse. We were there for a very short period of time. And then we were sent to the Modateks factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who accompanied you in the van to Modateks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Stuka, the JNA soldier who saved me, was in that van. Then there was a JNA soldier Mujdzan, that was his nickname. Also, there was the doctor's son, Dr. Ivankovic's son. That is to say, also a Serb, who was in the enemy army. Then Dr. Ivankovic -- I see the transcript in front of me. Ivankovic, I-v-a-n-k-o-v-i-c. I think there was another one there, too, but I cannot remember his name or his nickname or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, Mr. President, is a video-clip. It's already been admitted. It's P1076.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, we're just going to play this video. We don't need sound. Ask you to look at the video and then I'll ask you a question. P1076.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, is there anything from this video that you recognise? Any of the people? We can play it again, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I can say -- we can play it, but I can answer the question. From what I saw very quickly, the soldier who was closing the hangar, I remember him from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's play it one more time and then we'll stop at a point where we can identify who it is you're describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So we're seeing one of them close the door. Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The one who is still holding on to the door. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How were you able to remember that you saw this person also at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, that's a person I remember. He was wearing the same at Ovcara, and he was always a bit particular because he always stood a bit to the side, carrying a rifle, never involved in any beatings. He was just watching everything with a serious look on his face, and I had the impression that he was distancing himself from all that was going on. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the witness has identified the person who is on the right-hand part of the screen. Unless Your Honours think that more identification is required, I'm prepared to move on. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about going back to a place called Modateks in the white van. I'm going to ask you some questions, but in the meantime we can get ready with 65 ter 2802, which is tab 19. It's another one of the photographs, 2802.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, you can put that up on the screen whenever you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Karlovic, can you describe for the Judges what this Modateks place was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It was a textile factory, making blankets, I think. Because I know when we entered that large room, it was full of tables with sewing machines on them. It was a small textile factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you said there were seven of you prisoners. Were there other people at this place when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a group of people, mainly civilians, women, children, and elderly men, the people who were supposed to go the next morning to be exchanged in Croatia. That's probably why we were brought to that warehouse. The plan must have been for us who had been spared to be transported, together with those civilians, to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now this is the night of the 20th of November. During that night, did anything take place?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's important to the fact that we stayed in Vukovar eventually. During that night, a group of several men came, headed by Bulidza. And as soon as they saw the seven of us, they threatened us not to go anywhere. They said we should be killed. They were insulting us, threatening us, saying that they would come to pick us up the next morning and kill us. After that, they left. We stayed there until the morning. The civilians were taken out early in the morning, and the seven of us stayed in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And then from this place at Modateks, that morning, did you -- you -- your group then moved across to the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Just to continue where I left off. The morning came. The seven of us were still there. The group headed by Bulidza came again. There were beatings, insults, threats. However, a man who was there, who was guarding us, took us under his wing. He was in charge of the civilians. He had several JNA soldiers with him. His nickname was Grandad, Deda. That's how others called him too. Later I found out his name was Jezdimir Stankovic. He convinced Bulidza and the others to leave us alone for a while, saying that we had clean the place up. He told Bulidza to -- came later. I can say looking back that that man saved our lives. Bulidza did as he asked, and after the mistreatments and after beating us, they left. And Grandad, probably to spare himself further problems with us, decide then to transport us to the Velepromet warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now this beating that you referred to by the Chetniks that morning at Modateks, during that -- while that was taking place were there any more direct threats made against you by anyone in his group?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the beatings were a threat, letting us know what would happen to us later. I even remember one particular man, Safet, who put a gun in my mouth. All these beatings had the purpose of letting us know that we would be killed. It didn't last long but it was very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when you were at the Velepromet -- when you arrived at Velepromet, I should say, did you see an incident involving an old man who was among the prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it while still standing in my column. I must say, when we arrived at Velepromet, there was already a group of people who had formed a column, and one man was taken out of our column, out of that group. They dragged him away and cut his throat with a broken bottle. That incident took place, perhaps, 30 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Looking now on the screen in front of you, Mr. Karlovic, do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I see Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you indicate with the pen the location where you were standing and where this incident occurred involving this man whose throat was cut.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I must say, the pen shows at least a centimetre more than I intended to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you just --

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I try again?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Maybe we can wipe -- if we can wipe the image and start over. Just wait a second, Mr. Karlovic. We'll start again. Okay. Just ... very good. Now --

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's closer to the larger dot, not the small one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just put an X there, if you can.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This is the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you've just put a dot on the -- on the photograph. What's that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's roughly where I was standing as that incident was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did the incident take place where you were standing, or was it taking place somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. They took him to the back. I can show you in which direction --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you put an X on that place.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Again, the pen slid a bit off, but that's approximately the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to just put the letter A by the place you were standing and a letter B by the place where the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Karlovic, just to save a little bit of time, because we do have your evidence, you were then put into a room called the Stolarija or the carpentry work-shop. Could you just place a circle around the approximate location of that place.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And put a letter C by that.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We tender this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 18; 65 ter 2725.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Karlovic, this Stolarija, approximately how much time, how long did you stay there on this day, which is now the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I was there for five or six hours after being taken out of the carpentry shop. Then I was taken away. I passed through --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, before we talk about when you were taken away. In this photograph, are you able to identify the location of this room you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The room is this one, but my pen is not leaving a mark. I don't know why ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, put a letter A on that location.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in that room, were you with anyone else who had come with the group of seven from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tihomir Perkovic was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know where any of the other people in this group were being held at that time?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There was another room - I'll mark it with B - that was the room facing ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now on the screen, we see, in between those two letters, what appears to be a door. Is that the door that you were -- you went through, to go in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the central room, in fact. This is the entrance, the central room, and from that room, we entered room A on the left and room B on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence, you talk about prisoners who were being taken out of these rooms by Chetniks. The question here is whether, in the course of this you observed whether there was any -- was there a particular procedure or how would this actually take place?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There's no procedure. The JNA military police was in charge of guarding us. However, the Chetniks had no problem entering the two rooms we were in and taking people out. Quite simply, the JNA military police, in co-operation with the Chetniks, had organised for those people to be taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The men that were taken out, were they instructed to do anything before leaving this building?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the people who were taken out had to take their clothes off. For instance, after somebody left from my room, they had to take their clothes off right behind the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who was the youngest person in your room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In my room, the youngest was a 14-year-old boy. Fourteen or so. He was also taken out. There were two brothers. First of all, they wanted to take out the elder brother, but after the younger brother started screaming and crying, holding on to him and not letting him go, they left the elder brother in the room and took the younger one, the 14-year-old one, instead. After leaving the room, he also had to take his clothes off. He was taken outside. We heard his crying, moaning. He was saying, It hurts. Don't do this to me. After that, we heard gun-shots. And then we didn't hear the voice of the child anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names or did you hear the names of any of these Chetniks who were taking these prisoners out?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: What sticks in my mind is that one was Dule. And the other was Sveto, or Stevo, or Stevan. I'm not sure. In any case, it was one and the same group, which, on that day, within those few hours, removed people from these two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What became of Mr. Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: He was taken out of my room. Unfortunately, the man I referred to by the nickname Sveto obviously knew him, knew Perkovic, and Sveto seemed very glad that he had found him. And I know today that after being taken out, Perkovic was killed. He did not survive the removal from that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at some point, you were taken out of this room. Could we please have tab 8, which is 2675.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Oh, I should tender this exhibit into evidence, Mr. President. This ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3004, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So tab 8, 65 ter 2675.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Karlovic, who was it that came for you and then took you out of this room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: A group of Chetniks came for me. On that day, during those few hours, they had not been at the Velepromet warehouse. They came for me, took me out, and took me on towards the house where I was later tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is one of the photographs you marked on during the Mrksic evidence. What does the arrow show here?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This arrow designates the road along which I was taken when Belgija came for me. Belgija is the nickname of the man who was leading me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what is the letter A?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That's the structure from which I was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on your way out of Velepromet during this -- on this path, did you happen to see any bodies?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw several corpses lying there, in the place just as you leave the yard of Velepromet close to the railways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence, you talk about being taken by this person Belgija to a house where you are -- you meet a larger group of Chetniks. Could you just give a brief description of what took place at this location.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was brought to a house where there were more than 20 Chetniks. After I was brought in, they rejoiced because, as they put it, they had just received a young Ustasha to have fun with. There was a table in the middle. There was drink and food on the table. I was sat down in the middle. A man holding me at gunpoint, holding a gun to my head, in fact was standing behind me all the time. To my right was this man Belgija. On the other side there was an older man. And then the mistreatment started. Beatings, insults. They spat at me. At one point, they took my clothes off, leaving me bare to the waste. And amid all this mistreatment and beatings, they cut me up and injured me seriously on my arm, back. They burned candles on my skin. Broke my nose. Threatened me. And among them was one woman who kept talking them into raping me. And after they raped me she would cut my genitals off. Her nickname was Daca. And all this was supposed to end with Belgija slitting my throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karlovic, just to be clear for the record, were you raped during this encounter?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then what -- what happened while this was taking place?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, a man came into the house. Now I know who he is. His nickname is Mare. His name is Marko Ljuboja. He took in the whole scene, saw what was going on. He said, What's all this? What's going on? Marko Ljuboja, I have to say, was also a member of a Chetnik unit. To be more precise, he was a member of Seselj's Chetniks. And after seeing what was being done to me he set out from that house, and I remember they were telling him, Oh don't do that. You are going to save him. You want to save him. And as he was leaving, he said, No, no, you just go on doing what you were doing. But eventually he came back with another man whose nickname was Kinez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off because it's just about time for the first court break. Just to wind up this topic then, it was Kinez and Mare then who succeeded in getting you out of this house with the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They managed with great difficulty to get me out, because it nearly came to a fire-fight between them. But they managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if Your Honours wish to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, this is our first break. We'll take 30 minutes and come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Ah, yes, I'm sorry, the security will escort you out of the courtroom. Sorry about that. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, I overlooked one thing in my outline that I quickly want to jump back to before we continue. And that would be to show you an image that is tab 13, 65 ter 2681. Now, Mr. Karlovic, this is one of the photos that you marked on during your Mrksic testimony so I'm not going to ask you to make any more markings on this. But if you could just give the Judges a brief description of what appears on this, in relation to your markings. First of all, where is this, I should ask?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This is the area of Ovcara where that hangar is, where we were brought to from the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you just give a brief description of the markings there, what they relate to.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I marked the column of buses. That is to say, their positions, where we were. I marked with a number 2 the place where I had contact with the soldier Stuka. And number 3 is the place in front of the hangar where the seven of us who had been saved stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to move back to my outline, Mr. Karlovic, and I'd now ask you to look at a short video-clip. It's already in evidence. It's P1729. We don't need the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone that you recognise in this clip, Mr. Karlovic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised Kinez, who, together with Mare, saved me from that house that I spoke about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apart from just yesterday, when -- when we met, had you ever seen this video-clip before?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I myself found it on YouTube as well. I saw it before too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could just play it one last time, and I'll ask if you can give us an indication of who it is that you've identified as Kinez.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Want to stop it or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: This. Now. Well, it's the man can you see here, the tall man in the back with a beret on his head. Would that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could have P1730, page 1, which is 65 ter 4885. For the record, Mr. President, the time code the witness has just spoken of relates -- is -- is from 2 hours, 49 minutes, 29.1 seconds. If we can have the photograph, please. Oh, is it up? My apologies. This is 65 ter 4885.1. I'm sorry, .2. 4885.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karlovic, we can work with this photograph. And so just for the record, with the pen and with the usher's assistance, could you just put a circle around the head of the person you have identified as Kinez.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3005, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was Kinez dressed like this when he came to that house with Mare when they got you away from those Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after these events from November of 1991, did you ever have any subsequent encounters with this person, Kinez?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I encountered him in the Belgrade trial for the crimes committed at Ovcara. I testified in Belgrade then. I recognised Kinez because the Court asked me to identify him and Marko. And I saw him then, for the first time, after 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall now what his -- what his real name is?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Milojevic, nickname Kinez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, having to watch the clock a little bit, Mr. Karlovic, so I apologise in advance if -- if I have to cut you off because I want to make sure we get through the outline in the time that's left. And you've testified about this in your Mrksic testimony already and so we don't need great detail. But eventually did you then end up back in this Stolarija at Velepromet; and, if so, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: After Kinez and Mare got me out of that house, yet again, I was returned under his escort and Mare's and there were some other JNA soldiers there. And I was returned to Velepromet and I stayed there for about three or four hours. And sometime before midnight, the JNA, together with some of their officers, moved all the people from Velepromet to the Vukovar barracks, and that's where we spent the night. I'm talking about the 21st of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And before then, the next day, the 22nd of November, after you came back to Velepromet, did you get any treatment for those wounds that you'd gotten during the encounter with the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the officer who transported all of us to the barracks, when he looked at me and when he saw all the injuries that I had, I was taken to see a doctor who dressed my wounds and helped me in every way he could. That is where I was given that aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next day, the 22nd of November, Mr. Karlovic, can you tell us what happened on that day? And on this subject, I'm going to ask for more details because you did not testify about this part in the Mrksic trial.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of November, in the morning hours, we were driven from the Vukovar barracks in a big bus between 60 and 70 of us. We were driven to Sremska Mitrovica. During our trip, we stopped at Negoslavci, Sid. At any rate, the Serbs, who lived in these places, would come out. Of course, we were met in a very hostile manner, swearing, insults, et cetera. Then we arrived at the Sremska Mitrovica prison. We were taken out of the bus, were taken to a sports hall. That's where we all had to strip totally. We were frisked. As far as I'm concerned personally, after they saw these wounds on me and after I told them where these wounds had come from, that was the first time I was brutally beaten in Sremska Mitrovica. After this beating -- so I was beaten while I was naked. After that beating, I was taken outside. I was the last one who remained in that hall. I was taken outside. And then we all had to lie in this field and the policemen, that is to say, the prison guards who worked at that prison, beat us, and there were a few military policemen there as well who also took part in the beating. The beating was extremely brutal. Somehow I had this misfortune since I was from Zagreb. They knew that I was from the National Guards Corps, and as soon as I uttered this sentence that I was cut up by Chetniks, I was given special treatment. After we were all beaten up, we were taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise. Let me stop you right there just to ask you a couple questions based on what you've said so far. You said it was a pretty large group of you then, or it was between 60 and 70 of you on this bus. Where had all these other people come from, or when were you put together with the other people who were then transported to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to go back to something to clarify the situation. Already at Velepromet most of us were there, the ones that I've been speaking about. When we arrived at the Vukovar barracks, that is to say that night on the 21st of November, late in the evening, when we arrived at the barracks, already in the barracks there were a few people. I don't know exactly how many. My estimate is that the people from Velepromet and the people that we already found at the barracks it wasn't more than some 70 persons. How do I make this estimate? On the basis of the bus because I know that this bus was full. Everybody was sitting down and there were other people standing too. So on the basis of that, I'm saying that that would be my estimate as to the number of persons involved. Would that do or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know where these other people came from, the people that you eventually joined with during this time at Velepromet at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where they came from but these were local people there Vukovar. Probably they were taken prisoner in different places. I don't have any specific information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms, if you recall, of those people who gave you the beating, the beatings on your arrival at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the prison guards wore classical blue police uniforms. And the military police had their camouflage uniforms, except that they also had these white belts and -- and shoulder straps. That's what they wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did both groups participate in the beating?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What kind of -- what were the conditions of your confinement? Where did they put you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: First, I was at a particular facility for a few days. I don't know how to define the facility. There were about 60 persons there. There were mattresses on the floor. The room was packed. After those initial few days, I was transferred to a big room in a different facility. There were about 180-something of us there. The room was full of beds. We had heating. It was winter time. Within that room, there was a separate toilet facility with a sink. We had three meals a day. Truth to tell, they were rather poor, but it was three meals. So people were taken out for interrogations regularly. During those interrogations, people would mostly be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when your group arrived, were you the first prisoners to arrive, or were there prisoners there already?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was among the last ones. There were many prisoners already in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did any of those other prisoners stay in the same room of about 180 people that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to ask you something now. You mean the group that arrived with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The group that arrived with you -- let me -- I'll start over. There were other prisoners there when you arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the time when I had just arrived, the first day. Yes, there were already prisoners that were at Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know where they had come from, what their path had been?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they could have only had the kind of path that I had taken, from Vukovar to Sremska Mitrovica. All of these were people who were from Vukovar, who lived in Vukovar, fought in Vukovar. There were quite a few civilians. Those were the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were all the prisoners held together in this room of 180?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was separated into that big room, we were all there together, 180 of us. I would just like to add something on my own, if I may. Maybe that will assist all of you. My transfer to this big room -- well, I didn't understand why that happened. Because I was transferred to this room, where all the people were the people who were taken prisoner at Mitnica. They had surrendered at Mitnica. This was an independent group, independent of the town of Vukovar itself. So from that first room where I was, I was separated into this facility, and I was put up with these 180-something persons who were all from Mitnica. I just wanted to explain that, in order to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. How long approximately, then, did you stay in this room of 180 people?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: About two months. Perhaps a couple of days longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during that period of time, did your group encounter any people from the Serb side, apart from the guards?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were taken out for interrogations all the time. We saw these guards. I would just like to mention a delegation that visited us. Perhaps it was already January 1992. It so happened that a delegation came to visit us from the then-occupied part of Croatia. I can't even remember what it was called, Western Srem or something like that. They came and visited us - I can go on - and I can say that Mr. Hadzic was in that delegation. I remember that. And there were a few more people with him. They toured this room. Mr. Goran Hadzic did not say anything. He just observed it and walked around. Some people who accompanied him said things to people, taunted them. Since these were people also from Vukovar, they knew our Croats from Vukovar so, simply, it could not have happened without these taunts, provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if -- or do you recall if Mr. Hadzic or this group was accompanied by any military personnel?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were escorted by the military police because they themselves wore uniforms too, camouflage uniforms. They themselves were in uniform, and the people who came with them, that is to say, the Yugoslav army people, they accompanied them. And also the military policemen who were guarding us were there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall how Mr. Hadzic was dressed?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give a detailed description now. But as far as I can remember, I think he was in uniform too and the entire delegation was. I think it was a camouflage uniform. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you were not from the Vukovar area so how did you know it was Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Goran Hadzic was not a person who was unknown in Croatia. I was involved in the war. I was involved in what was happening. Irrespective of my age, I knew very well who Goran Hadzic was. Also, in addition to that, there were people in my room who were from Vukovar, who knew him, and there was no way I could have made a mistake, not known. So it's those two reasons. I can also just add that I remember his arrest in Plitvice. This was in the media. That's why I'm saying that he was well-known in Croatia, as far as the Serb rebellion with concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At some point, were you and the others registered with the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, we were transferred from these other rooms to the first rooms that I had come from. And then we were registered with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How long approximately did you stay in this room of 180? I may have asked you this already.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have asked me already. I spent about two months in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And from there, then, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We went to another facility, another room, where we were registered by the Red Cross. Evidently there was a reason why we had been separated for a while and hidden in those rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then when you moved to this third location, third location within Sremska Mitrovica, can you just briefly describe for us the conditions during that period.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the conditions were similar to the ones that were there before. It was a smallish room, 60 persons, a lot of commotion. We slept like sardines. I repeat again: We had three small meals per day. We had heating during the winter. We had a toilet facility with a sink where we could get water. There were interrogations that took place every day. We were beaten during the interrogations because they would always find a reason to beat people. And I can say that in addition to it the fact that we were squeezed into that room and that we had very little food, the greatest problem was this torture, these beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall which personnel were involved in these interrogations and beatings, what units or groups they were part of?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the entire process of interrogation was carried out by intelligence officers. There were officers. They even introduced themselves by rank, from captain, major, colonel. There were even some non-commissioned ranks. Mainly those were JNA officers. The beatings were somehow divided between the military policemen, that is to say soldiers, and sometimes even the officers beat people themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During the time when Mr. Hadzic came with the delegation, did any members of the delegation make statements about what they -- what would happen, what was planned for those of you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you about a question that a person, a man from that delegation, asked. He asked, How are you doing? Is it warm enough for you here? Some people answered, Yes, yes. And then he added, You will be warmer when you come to us. One man was holding a cigarette, and he asked one of us, Croats, How about putting out this cigarette in the palm of your hand? But fortunately that did not happen. There were other provocations, more taunts from other people from the entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the statement about things getting warmer when you went to them. Was there any more information or indication of what was intended? What did they intend would take place?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Quite simply, we somehow got this information that our group was supposed to be transferred to that Autonomous District of Western Srem for the trial that was supposed to be -- take place in Vukovar. We -- we had that information. And the visit of that delegation, including Goran Hadzic and his team, and all those words, and little provocations could only be a confirmation of that. After we were all registered by the International Red Cross, we became aware that that, indeed, was the plan, that a group from Sremska Mitrovica be transferred to Vukovar for that new trial or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you eventually ever transferred back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. After I was registered by the Red Cross, on the 22nd of May, 1992, I was exchanged in an all-for-all exchange, and that was the end of the story with Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Karlovic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Goran Hadzic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to stick to two subjects you testified about. First of all, I will ask you to provide some clarification concerning your testimony about your stay at Ovcara. As I understood your testimony, you were there while it was still day, so you were able to observe what was going on around you.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said you had set off from Ovcara when it was already getting dark.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a report we received from the astronomical observatory because I know you were hard put to define a time frame as to when you came and when you left. And you will see that on the 20th of November the time of sunrise and sunset.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D89, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are reports for the 19th, 20th, and 21st. We are interested in the 20th because you were there on the 20th of November. And you'll see in line 3 the time of sunset, it's 1610 hours. And the duration of dusk is until 1644. And then the night begins. Can you tell me, in view of the various times you mentioned from memory, would you agree that you could have left Ovcara at this time, when dusk begins approximately, or while it was still only getting dark, during dusk, before 1645 -- 4?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
